Database Programming Fundamentals

Learn how modern applications manage persistent data across networks.

Welcome to the course. Today we bridge the gap between C# code and relational data storage.

Agenda

  • Client-Server Architecture
  • Software Layers and APIs
  • Relational Database Structure
  • Table Relationships
  • SQL Fundamentals (CRUD)
  • Filtering and Sorting
  • Joining Multiple Tables
We will cover everything from hardware architecture to writing your first SQL joins.

Client-Server Architecture

  • Clients: Workstations or mobile devices
  • Network: LAN, WAN, or Internet
  • Server: Powerful machine hosting data
  • Supports multi-user distributed systems
Unlike local apps, business systems distribute processing across multiple hardware components.

Database Software Layers

  • Application: C# WinForms or Maui
  • Data Access API: ADO.NET/Entity Framework
  • DBMS: SQL Server or MySQL
  • Physical Database: The data file
The API acts as the bridge, translating your C# commands into SQL for the database engine.

Relational Database Structure

  • Tables represent entities (nouns)
  • Rows represent individual records
  • Columns represent specific attributes
  • Primary Keys uniquely identify rows
Think of tables as spreadsheets where every row is a unique instance of an object like a Customer.

Primary Key Best Practices

  • Use auto-generated 'identity' integers
  • Avoid using names or emails
  • IDs remain stable over time
  • Safest way to target rows
Identity columns ensure every record has a unique ID without manual input from the user.

Table Relationships

  • One-to-Many: Most common type
  • One-to-One: Specific detail records
  • Many-to-Many: Requires junction tables
  • Foreign Keys link related tables
Relationships allow us to connect data, like linking many customers to one specific city.

SQL Fundamentals (CRUD)

  • Select: Read data
  • Insert: Create data
  • Update: Modify data
  • Delete: Remove data
SQL is the standard language used to perform these four essential data operations.

Basic Select Statement

SELECT * FROM customers;
The asterisk is a wildcard that retrieves every column from the specified table.

Filtering and Sorting

SELECT ProductName, Price, Stock 
FROM Products 
WHERE Price < 50 
ORDER BY Price DESC;
The WHERE clause filters rows, while ORDER BY organizes the results for the user.

Joining Multiple Tables

  • Combine data from different tables
  • Use Inner Joins for matches
  • Table aliases improve readability
  • Join on Primary/Foreign key pairs
Aliases like 'C' for Customers make complex queries much easier to write and maintain.

Inner Join Example

SELECT C.CustomerName, O.OrderDate 
FROM Customers AS C 
INNER JOIN Orders AS O 
ON C.CustomerID = O.CustomerID;
This query links customers to their orders by matching their unique ID numbers.

Inserting New Data

INSERT INTO Products (ProductName, Price) 
VALUES ('Wireless Keyboard', 49.99);
When inserting, ensure the value order matches the column order defined in the statement.

Updating Existing Records

UPDATE Customers 
SET Email = 'new@example.com' 
WHERE CustomerID = 1;
Always use the Primary Key in the WHERE clause to avoid updating the wrong person.

Deleting Data Safely

DELETE FROM Products 
WHERE ProductID = 7;
Deletion is permanent; double-check your filters before executing this command.

Critical Safety Warning

  • Missing WHERE affects every row
  • Update without WHERE ruins data
  • Delete without WHERE clears tables
  • Always verify your filter first
Omitting a WHERE clause is a common and catastrophic mistake for beginner developers.

Key Takeaways

  • Apps use APIs for databases
  • Primary Keys ensure data integrity
  • SQL handles all CRUD operations
  • WHERE clauses prevent data loss
  • Joins connect related entity tables
Mastering these fundamentals is the first step toward building professional multi-user applications.
